title: THE CHORUS THAT COULD NOT HEAR ITSELF
deck: A flock of ten thousand singers has locked onto one note so loud that it is cracking the ice shelf under the town of Lowmark, and the council will fire a pulse array at dawn on the eighth day. Illuminara has to learn what a mind that cannot speak is actually doing, and to do it without becoming the louder noise.
shape: Six scenes across eight days: a note nobody can name; a room too loud to hear in; forty minutes of quiet on the ice; a clean tone that makes things worse, and why; a child at the edge of the thick ice, and a prediction that is allowed to fail; and a town that learns to keep its own hum down.

scenes.title: A Note Like a Held Breath
paragraphs: *Marrow Shelf above the town of Lowmark, Halden · Day 1, 07:40*

The note was not loud so much as total. Illuminara felt it first in the plates of her breastbone, then in the soles of her boots, and only a half second later as a sound, as though her ears had been the last part of her to hear it. Overhead the ring-singers hung in a slow wheel against the green-black sky, ten thousand pale hoops each the width of a doorway, and every one of them was holding the same low note.

Pia Raskin met her at the end of the sled track with a recorder in a fur sack and a headset round her neck. She was twenty-four and had not slept, and she spoke the way people speak when they have been right for months and have stopped expecting it to help.

**Pia Raskin** 
Forty-one hertz, give or take a breath. It was a chord until eleven weeks ago. Then it was a ladder, a few voices a step apart. Then it was this.

A man in a council coat was already walking out across the ice toward them with a tablet held against his chest like a shield. He was past sixty, broad, careful on his feet. He did not offer his hand.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Councillor Brandt. You're the one the acoustician wrote to. Look at this before you decide what to think.

The tablet showed the shelf in section: a slab of ice a hundred metres thick, the town of eight thousand on its landward half, and a pale line running through it a kilometre out from the first streets, dated in an engineer's hand.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Four metres of new fracture since Tuesday. The geologists give the shelf eight days before the crack reaches the pumping district, and after that it is not a crack, it is a decision made by the ice. The north rim has a pulse array, built for avalanches. Day eight, at dawn, I fire it, the flock goes up the valley, and the shelf gets its rest.

**Pia Raskin** 
It's one animal. Break it and you don't get ten thousand birds. You get ten thousand things that can't find the song.

**Ewan Brandt** 
A flock that can't tell me what it's doing is not a partner, Miss Raskin. It is a hazard with wings, and I will not wait for the ice to prove you right.
Illuminara looked at the wheel of singers and then at the line on the tablet, and did not argue with either of them.

**Illuminara** 
He's right about the hazard. The fracture is following the note, and the note won't stop because we ask it nicely. I won't ask you to wait for the ice, Councillor. I'll ask for eight days, and I'll tell you now that for the first of them I'll be nearly useless. I don't know yet what it's doing.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Can't you simply ask it?

**Illuminara** 
Nothing in it answers to my language, and I can't reach into a mind and read it. If I could, I'd be the thing you were right to be afraid of. What I can do is listen longer than you can afford to, and stand where the ice is thin.
Brandt weighed that for the length of one breath of the note, which was a long time.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Day eight, dawn. Until then you have the ice. If the crack passes the red stakes on the north side I fire, and you don't stop me.

**Illuminara** 
Agreed. If I'm about to stop you, I will have been wrong first.

scenes.title: A Room Too Loud to Hear In
paragraphs: *Pia's recording shed, an old pump house on the shelf edge · Day 1, 13:20*
The shed smelled of coolant, and eleven months of recordings were stacked along its walls. Pia pulled up the last three days and let Illuminara look without explaining.

**Pia Raskin** 
Here's my reading. Something frightened them: a predator, a quake, something under the ice. They gathered on one note because that's the alarm they have, and when the alarm doesn't end, they get louder.

**Illuminara** 
What would a predator look like in this? Is there one?
Pia scrolled back across seventy-two hours for a flock turning, a sweep, a sudden peak in the pitch. The line was flat as a ruled edge.

**Pia Raskin** 
No. It just keeps getting louder.

**Illuminara** 
Then I'd like to stop asking what they're saying and ask what they're doing. Can you show me one singer? Not the flock. One, and the two beside it.

It took Pia forty minutes to pull three neighbours out of the mix, each from its own ring-mounted tag. When she laid the traces over one another, Illuminara watched them for a while without speaking. In the spring recordings the three had sat almost on top of one another, a tenth of a hertz apart, like three hands holding the same rope. In the last week they sat three whole hertz apart, and each swung up and down in volume as it tried to find the others.

**Illuminara** 
They're not holding a note. They're chasing each other's note, and the chase is getting louder.

**Pia Raskin** 
That's what I said. They're panicking.

**Illuminara** 
Or they're doing what you'd do in a room where you can't hear the person next to you. What do you do? And what does the room do?
Pia opened her mouth, and closed it again. Outside, the note leaned on the walls of the shed.

**Pia Raskin** 
Speak up. And it gets louder. Everyone's shouting over everyone. It feeds itself.

**Illuminara** 
Then the question is what filled the room. Something is sitting on their band. Wind, ice, a current under the shelf. Or us.

Pia was already dragging a second window across the screen. The shelf's own geophones had recorded a faint steady hum at the edge of the town for weeks, which nobody had read as anything but infrastructure. It began eleven weeks ago, the same week as the ladder.

**Pia Raskin** 
The new pumping district. District four. They switched it on in August. It's a hum at forty-two hertz. It's right on them.
Brandt had come in without knocking and was standing behind them with snow melting off his shoulders. He read the screen with his mouth set.

**Ewan Brandt** 
August is also when the warm spell started, and when the fish run moved north. You have three coincidences and one flock.

**Illuminara** 
I do. I'd drop two of them if I could find a test that only one could pass. Is anything about district four going to change soon, without anyone having to change it for us?
Brandt looked at the ceiling as if the answer were written there, and then, grudgingly, at his watch.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Impeller swap. 02:10 tonight, forty minutes, district four only. It's been on the schedule for a month. You can listen to it all night if you like. Listening costs me nothing.

scenes.title: Forty Minutes of Quiet
paragraphs: *The shelf edge, district four, a hundred metres from the fracture · Day 2, 02:05*

They went out at two in the morning in sealed coats, Illuminara and Pia, with a second geophone planted in the ice at the edge of the ring's shadow. The singers hung overhead, faintly luminous in the dark. With her palm against the ice Illuminara could feel the shelf sing back, a long shudder through bone-deep cold.
At 02:10 the hum in the geophone stopped. It did not fade. It simply was not there, like a clock one has stopped hearing and is suddenly aware of.

**Pia Raskin** 
District four's off.
For nine seconds nothing changed. Then the traces on Pia's screen began to move. The three neighbours, the same three, slid toward one another along the frequency axis like beads along a string.

**Pia Raskin** 
Spread's closing. Three hertz, two, one point five. Volume's falling. Down four decibels. Five.

Overhead, the ring was changing shape. The singers on its eastern arc tightened, and the great wheel lost its raggedness and began to turn in a smooth slow circle. The note under it did something Illuminara had never heard from an organism. It came apart into three voices, a low one and a middle one and a high one, each a clear step from the next, and held there, sounding like a chord.

**Pia Raskin** 
That's the old chord. That's the spring chord.

It lasted eleven minutes. Then, at 02:21, the spread began to widen again. The voices drifted into one another and the chord blurred and the note thickened back toward the single wall of sound. Pia swore and held her hands out, as if to catch it.

**Pia Raskin** 
Nothing's turned on. Four is still off.

**Illuminara** 
They've lost their reference. A chord keeps itself in tune because everyone can hear everyone. The quiet gave them eleven minutes of that and they spent it. With nothing steady in the room to settle against, they drift back to the only habit they have left: lock onto the loudest thing and hold.

**Pia Raskin** 
Which is the note.

**Illuminara** 
Which is themselves, as loudly as possible.
At 02:50 district four came back on, and the hum came back with it, and the spread opened like a hand. By 03:00 the old wall of sound was whole.

Brandt was waiting at the sled track in a thermal coat over his pyjamas, with a mug going cold in his hand. He had watched the screen on the council relay from his kitchen. He did not pretend otherwise.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Five decibels. For eleven minutes. And the crack grew two centimetres while you were having your concert.

**Illuminara** 
It did. The shelf lags behind the sound. It doesn't answer in minutes.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Then you have one night of data and a pause I'd have scheduled in any case. And you're about to ask me to turn off the heat for a quarter of my town on a theory.

**Illuminara** 
I am. I'll tell you what the theory costs before I ask. How long can a district stay off?

**Ewan Brandt** 
Ahlgren will tell you. The loop engineer.
Tove Ahlgren was a thin woman with a woollen cap and a voice like a grating hinge, and she gave the answer without being asked twice.

**Tove Ahlgren** 
Glycol in the district loop goes to slush at minus sixty. At this temperature that's seventy minutes with the pumps dead, and I will not sign for seventy. Fifty-five. One district at a time. And not the same one two nights running, or the return lines freeze and I'm digging them out with my hands. Four tonight means four again on Day 4 and not before.

**Ewan Brandt** 
What do you do with fifty-five minutes? Watch them hold a chord, and then watch it fall apart?

**Illuminara** 
No. The chord falls apart because nothing in the room is steady. I want to give them something steady: one clean tone, quiet, right on forty-one, for them to settle against the way a choir settles against a pitch pipe.
Brandt rubbed his jaw. Pia was holding her breath; Illuminara could hear it.

**Ewan Brandt** 
If you're wrong, the crack runs while my pumps are off and my people are cold.

**Illuminara** 
Yes.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Then you do it once. And the cannons stay loaded, and my thumb stays on the switch.

scenes.title: The Louder Noise
paragraphs: *The shelf rim, the town's emergency speaker array · Day 4, 17:50*

She built the tone with Pia on the town's alarm array, nine horn speakers along the shelf rim that warned the harbour in whiteout. She tuned it to forty-one hertz, as clean as a sine wave could be made on equipment never meant for it, and set its level twenty decibels below the flock's note: a pitch pipe, not a voice. Tove Ahlgren shut district four's pumps at 17:55, so that the town's own hum was out of the room and the tone would be the only thing that had changed.

By 17:58 the ring had found its chord again without her, the old three steps, a little ragged. Illuminara walked out onto the thin ice thirty metres from the fracture and set her palms on the surface.

**Pia Raskin** 
On your word.

**Illuminara** 
Go.
The tone came out over the ice, steady and bare. For six seconds nothing happened. Illuminara found she was holding her own breath, and made herself let it go.
Then the flock answered.

It was not what she had hoped. The chord, which had stood for two minutes, went to pieces. The ring above them seemed to flinch, and the spread on Pia's screen snapped wide. The singers surged up the frequency axis toward the tone, every voice at once, and the note thickened and rose, six decibels, seven, ten.

**Pia Raskin** 
They're matching it. They're matching it, and they're getting louder.

**Tove Ahlgren** 
Crack's moving. Thirty centimetres. Forty. It's going.

The sound that came up through the ice was not a note. It was a rifle shot, long and slow, and a seam opened in the white a body's length from Illuminara's hand and ran away from her toward the red stakes.

She did the one thing she could do alone. She put her whole weight onto the ice and held it, the way one holds a door against a wind, and the seam stopped, shuddering, two stakes short of where it would have forced Brandt's thumb.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Tone off. Tone off now.

The horns went silent. The flock's note stood a moment in the dark, wide and ragged, and then began to settle. Illuminara stayed on her knees on the ice with her palms flat. Her hands were shaking and she did not hide it.
Brandt came out across the rim in the dusk with his cannon-remote in his fist, and he stopped a body's length from her and did not use it.

**Ewan Brandt** 
That is the thing I told you.

**Illuminara** 
Yes. It's exactly the thing you told me. I made myself the louder noise.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Forty centimetres.

**Illuminara** 
Forty-one.

Pia had come out behind them with her headset down around her neck. She had been crying and was not embarrassed about it. Illuminara looked at the ring, where the singers were still settling, and went on talking slowly, the way one works a sum aloud so that other people can stop her.

**Illuminara** 
I'll say why, because the next try depends on it. I gave them something perfect: a pure tone, from far off, at one level, reaching ten thousand singers in the same instant. A choir doesn't tune that way. It tunes along a chain, each singer listening to the one beside it, and the chain carries the pitch. I skipped the chain, so every link tried to answer a stranger at once. And they had found their chord by themselves before I started. Silence gave them eleven minutes. I gave them an order, and they obeyed it.

**Pia Raskin** 
So a better speaker won't do it.

**Illuminara** 
A worse one might. Something small enough that only the nearest singer can hear it isn't a stranger to anyone. It's a neighbour to one, and the chain does the rest. And it has to waver a little. Nothing in that ring is perfectly steady, and a perfectly steady note isn't a voice. Pia, what does the ring carry above its note?

**Pia Raskin** 
Overtones, all the way up. They tune to ratios. Every singer sits on a harmonic of the one beside it.

**Illuminara** 
Then the same note four octaves up is already a harmonic of the ring. A high voice they've always had room for.

**Ewan Brandt** 
A theory with a person in it.

**Illuminara** 
A theory that makes a prediction the tone didn't. If I'm right, the first singer to answer is the one nearest the player, at the rim, within the first few notes. Then the change travels round the arc one neighbour at a time, later the farther it goes, like a rumour. If the whole ring moves at once, I'm wrong, and we stop.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Who's the person?

**Pia Raskin** 
Ingrid Ahl's girl. Sunniva. She's nine, and she plays a tin flute because she can't carry a tune with her voice. She says it comes out flat whatever she does.

**Illuminara** 
Flat is good. If her mother says yes and she says yes, I'd want her on the thick ice, thirty metres from the seam, with her mother beside her and me between her and the crack. If either of them says no, I do something else, and I haven't got a second thing yet.
Brandt looked at the seam, and at the stakes, and at the remote in his hand.

**Ewan Brandt** 
I want to hear them say it. Not you. Them.

scenes.title: A Child at the Edge of the Thick Ice
paragraphs: *The Ahl family kitchen, then the shelf · Day 5, 16:40*

Ingrid Ahl made them tea. She was a short, square woman who repaired harbour nets, and she listened with her hands round her cup while Pia told her all of it, including the forty-one centimetres. Then she looked at her daughter, who was on the floor putting a cat into a box.

**Ingrid Ahl** 
Sunniva. Did you hear?

**Sunniva Ahl** 
They sing too loud and the ice breaks. I have to play so they can hear each other.

**Ingrid Ahl** 
You don't have to. That's the whole point of asking.
Sunniva turned the tin flute over in her hands.

**Sunniva Ahl** 
I won't play it at them. That's like humming at a baby that's already crying. I'll play it next to them. Quietly. Like I'm a singer too.

**Illuminara** 
Will you play it for me the way you'd play it if nobody were listening? Not clean. However it comes out.

Sunniva put the flute to her lip. What came out was thin, slightly flat, and wavered at the end of every breath like a candle in a draught. Pia, in the doorway, laughed and put her hand over her mouth.

**Illuminara** 
That. Don't fix it.

**Sunniva Ahl** 
Mum says it sounds like a kettle that's tired.

**Illuminara** 
Then be a tired kettle. If it comes out too good, they'll know it isn't one of them.

**Ingrid Ahl** 
Thirty metres from the line, no further, and I'm holding the rope. If I say we go, she goes. If I say stop, there's no argument, and Ewan Brandt can put that in his book.
Brandt had not come in, but he was standing in the hallway with his coat on, and he did not pretend not to have heard.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Noted. Both.

*Day 6, 17:55.* In the control room, which smelled of machine oil and old coffee, Tove Ahlgren stood at the loop board with her thumb over the breaker for district four. Brandt had given her the order himself and then, after thinking about it, had put his own hand beside hers on the cold metal.

**Tove Ahlgren** 
It's your thumb on the town's heat tonight, Ewan, not mine.

**Ewan Brandt** 
I know whose it is.
He threw the breaker himself. The hum that had lived in the floor of the town for eleven weeks went out of it, and in the quiet that followed the room sounded like a held breath.

Out on the ice the light was going. Ingrid knelt in her net-mender's coat with the rope in her fist. Sunniva stood on the thick ice, thirty metres from the old seam, with the tin flute against her lip and her eyes on the flock. Illuminara knelt between them and the crack with her palms on the surface. Pia's screen glowed on a sled beside her, one trace picked out in red: the singer nearest the child, a hoop at the rim no larger than the others.
The ring found its chord on its own, as it always did, and held it for ten minutes. Then, at 18:06, the spread began to widen.

**Illuminara** 
Now. That's all the quiet they get alone.

The first note was so quiet she thought she had imagined it, a thin, slightly flat E, four octaves above the ring's low note, the sound of a child's breath on a metal pipe. It carried a few metres and was gone. The ring went on blurring. Sunniva took a breath and played it again. Nothing.

**Pia Raskin** 
Not a flicker, anywhere.

**Illuminara** 
Again. Quiet things need saying twice.
On the third note the red trace dipped. The singer at the rim slid down a quarter of a hertz, as though it had heard something and wished to be polite.

**Pia Raskin** 
The nearest one. Only the nearest one.

**Illuminara** 
Watch the next. It should lag.

**Pia Raskin** 
Two seconds. The one beside it has gone. Now the next, four seconds. It's walking round the arc.

The change ran away along the ring like a rumour, neighbour to neighbour, each hoop tuning itself against the one beside it and carrying it on, later the farther it went. Illuminara found that she was smiling, and that her palms were not shaking at all.

**Pia Raskin** 
Spread's closing again. Two hertz. One. Down eight decibels.

**Tove Ahlgren** 
Crack is holding. Hold, hold. It's holding.

**Pia Raskin** 
Oh, listen. Listen to it.

The chord that had always failed by now did not fail. It was not as clean as the spring recordings, and several of the voices wavered, but it was a chord, three clear steps and a low shimmer under them, like a bell that has been struck properly at last. The shelf under Illuminara's hands, which for three weeks had felt like a drum with a tight skin, loosened by a degree she could actually feel.

Sunniva went on playing, softly, her cheeks red, her mother's hand on her shoulder. When Tove called time at 18:50 the chord was still standing, forty-four minutes past the point where it had always failed, and the child lowered the flute.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Ahlgren, bring four back on. Slowly.
The hum returned to the shelf the way a tide returns. The chord blurred and stayed a chord, a little frayed, for another twenty minutes before the old ragged lean began to creep back.

scenes.title: Two Tenants
paragraphs: *The council chamber, Lowmark · Day 7, 20:15*
They argued until midnight, and nobody won. That was the way Illuminara knew it was real.

**Ewan Brandt** 
One hour a night is not a policy. It is a hope. My loop engineer can't run a district dark more than every second night without her pipes freezing, and every night we cool one, the people in it are cold.

**Illuminara** 
I'm asking for less than that, if it can be done, and I can't promise it. Last night proved a mechanism. It did not prove a cure. The flock slid back toward its wall within twenty minutes of the pumps coming on. What we need is for the town to stop being the thing that fills the room.

**Tove Ahlgren** 
The pump is the problem, not the hour. Forty-two hertz is the impeller blade rate. I can slow the new impellers in district four and move their hum down to thirty-one. That's below the flock's band, it's inside what the loop can bear, and it costs me nine days of work and a part that's only in the harbour depot.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Nine days is past the dawn I gave you.

**Illuminara** 
Then we cover the nine days. A dusk hour every second evening, district four, with Sunniva or one of Pia's students playing at the edge if they choose to, and the shelf watched. On the nights between, Tove?

**Tove Ahlgren** 
I can run four at reduced flow, same blade speed. The hum stays on forty-two but sits a good twelve decibels quieter, and the loop stays warm enough. That's what I can give you. Dark twice running I can't.

**Illuminara** 
A quieter hum buys time, not a cure. And the cannons stay loaded until the hum is down. I don't ask you to unload them on faith.

**Pia Raskin** 
The students will need to be asked, not told. Some won't want to be out there. That's their right.

**Ewan Brandt** 
And the midnight haul.

There was a murmur among the benches. The midnight haul was the town's old tradition, the net crews going out under floodlights while the water pumps ran at full speed. A third of the town earned its winter on it.

**Illuminara** 
The haul runs at the loudest hour of the pumps. That hour has to move. I don't know what it will cost the crews to move it, and I won't pretend to. I'd like the people who do the haul to say how it could move, and what they would need. If they can't make it work, the cannons are yours, and I won't stop you.
Ingrid Ahl stood up at the back. She had not been invited to speak and it didn't seem to occur to her to ask.

**Ingrid Ahl** 
My crews will move the haul to the grey hour before dawn. It's worse fishing. We'll lose a quarter of the catch. But I've sat on that ice since I was Sunniva's age, and I've never once heard the sound I heard the other night. If a quarter of the catch is the price of that, I'll sign for it.
The vote was nineteen to six. Brandt was one of the six, and he said so clearly, for the record.

**Ewan Brandt** 
I am voting against the unloading of the array. I will vote for the pump, and the dusk hour, and the haul. I believe in all of it as far as the evidence goes. The evidence does not go far enough for me to take the cannons off the rim, and I won't pretend that it does.

**Illuminara** 
That's the right place for you to stand, Councillor. I'd think less of the plan if you weren't standing there.

At dawn on day eight the array stood loaded on the north rim, a squat row of barrels pointed at the valley. Brandt came out alone in the grey light with a technician and a clipboard, and did not look at Illuminara until he had stood a while beside the first barrel.

**Ewan Brandt** 
I told you I would fire this at dawn. The crack has not moved in thirty-six hours.

**Illuminara** 
Not since the flute. It may move again. One hour a night is a hope, as you said, and I'd rather you kept your hand on that switch than took it off.

**Ewan Brandt** 
I am not firing. I am not unloading, either. I will tell the technician when.

It took ten days, not nine. Tove Ahlgren lost a day to a snowstorm on the harbour road and swore at the depot until it gave her the part, and she put the slow impellers into district four with her own hands. The hum in the floor of Lowmark came down to thirty-one hertz on the tenth dusk, below the band, and the flock's note over the shelf was a chord and not a wall.

The price was not paid by the town in general. On every second cold dusk the families on the top streets of district four carried their bedding down to the schoolhouse and slept on cots in the gymnasium, and on the grey mornings Illuminara went down to the harbour, where Ingrid's crew was hauling a thin net in the half-dark.

**Ingrid Ahl** 
A quarter short, as I said. Mine to be short. The ice sounds like ice again. I've stopped being able to remember when it sounded like anything else.
Ahlgren came down the quay with a flask, grey in the face from three nights on a cot, and took one handle of the net without asking.

**Tove Ahlgren** 
A boy up on the cots asked me why the floor wasn't humming. I told him it was a favour. He said it was a bad favour. He'll get used to it in a week. I'll be sorry for the week.

Not all of the ring had come back. A fifth of it, some two thousand singers, had drifted up the valley in the worst of the loud weeks and did not rejoin. Pia followed their tags for three days before the mountain took the signal.

**Pia Raskin** 
I keep wondering whether they can hear each other up there. The ones that left.

**Illuminara** 
Each one can hear its nearest. It's the only thing the ring ever needed.

On the eleventh morning Brandt walked out to the north rim again, alone, and this time the technician was already waiting with his clipboard. Overhead, in the first light, the ring-singers wheeled in their slow circle and the sound they made was ten thousand slightly different voices, none of them wanting to be louder than its neighbour, all of them in tune. It was a little like rain on a tin roof, if rain could keep its pitch.

**Ewan Brandt** 
Unload it. All twelve. And log it under my name.

The technician began to turn the first breech. Brandt did not watch him. He stood with his head tilted, the way a man listens who has spent his life being right about the weather and has just heard something he did not expect to hear.

critic_line: Ten thousand ring-singers were chasing one another's note until it cracked the ice under Lowmark; Illuminara learned they had lost the neighbour who could hear them, failed once by becoming the louder noise, then let a nine-year-old's tired tin flute and a town's own choices bring the chord back and the cannons down.
